gloss: each other; by yourself, your own
title: saling and sendiri
pattern: saling + verb (each other) · verb + sendiri (by yourself) · noun + sendiri (your own)
explanation: saling goes before a verb to make it mutual: Kami saling membantu (We help each other). English puts 'each other' after the verb, but Indonesian puts saling in front and needs nothing after. sendiri after a verb means by yourself, on your own: Saya pergi sendiri (I'm going on my own), Dia tinggal sendiri (She lives alone). After a noun it means your own: kamar sendiri (a room of your own), rumah sendiri (a home of your own). After a person it's '-self', for emphasis: Saya sendiri belum pernah ke sana (I've never been there myself).
natural: Saling kenal (to know each other) comes up whenever people are introduced: Sudah saling kenal? Travelling alone, you'll often be asked Sendiri saja? or Sendirian? (On your own?), usually out of friendly concern.
stiff: satu sama lain also means each other, but it sounds written; in conversation, saling is what people say. And sendiri doesn't mean lonely: for that the word is kesepian.

examples.english: The neighbours here help each other out.

gap.why: 'Each other' is saling, before the verb.

examples.cultureNote: Gotong royong, neighbours pitching in together, is a value Indonesians are proud of, from cleaning the street to helping at a wedding.

gap.why: After a verb, sendiri means on your own.

examples.registerNotes: A reply to Sama siapa? (Who are you here with?). Sendirian stresses that nobody else came at all.

examples.english: They've known each other for a long time.

gap.why: Knowing each other is mutual, so saling goes before kenal.

examples.indonesian: Sekarang saya sudah punya kamar sendiri.
examples.english: I've got a room of my own now.

gap.why: After a noun, sendiri means your own; kamar saya would just be 'my room'.
